title: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
summary: How dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN with a fixed-size matrix memory, why that memory fills up, and how the delta rule and gating (Gated DeltaNet) fix it.
outcomes: Explain why linear attention can run as an RNN with a constant-size state instead of a growing KV cache
Compute the state updates of linear attention, DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet by hand on a toy sequence
Explain why additive memory collides and how the delta rule and the decay gate each fix a different failure
Compare the parallel, recurrent and chunkwise forms and say which one is used for training and for decoding
Estimate the memory saved by a hybrid model such as Qwen3-Next that mixes Gated DeltaNet with attention

lessons.title: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN

blocks.md:
Recall from the attention course: each output is a softmax-weighted average of value vectors, with weights from query-key dot products. During generation the model keeps every past key and value (the **KV cache**), so memory per sequence grows linearly with context length and each new token must read all of it.

Linear attention asks: can we summarize the past in a **fixed-size state** instead, like an RNN, without giving up parallel training?

blocks.title: Numbers stored per head: KV cache vs a d x d state

scenes.caption: Softmax attention stores a key and a value (d numbers each) per past token, so storage is 2Ld and keeps growing. A d x d state stays flat.
With d = 128 the two cross at L = 64 tokens. At 262,144 tokens the KV cache holds 67,108,864 numbers per head versus 16,384 for the state.
Larger heads raise the flat line (d^2) and move the break-even point right, but it is still tiny compared with long contexts.

blocks.md: Katharopoulos et al. (2020) write attention with a general similarity: $o_i = \sum_j \text{sim}(q_i,k_j)v_j / \sum_j \text{sim}(q_i,k_j)$. Softmax uses $\text{sim}=\exp(q^\top k/\sqrt{d})$. If instead $\text{sim}(q,k)=\phi(q)^\top\phi(k)$ for some **feature map** $\phi$, matrix products can be regrouped: $(\phi(Q)\phi(K)^\top)V = \phi(Q)(\phi(K)^\top V)$. The right side never builds the $L \times L$ matrix. They used $\phi(x)=\text{elu}(x)+1$ to keep similarities positive.

Later work simplified further: drop the denominator (it caused numerical instability) and use $\phi$ = identity, as the DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet papers do in their notation. With a causal mask, the output for token $t$ is then:

blocks.tex: o_t=\sum_{i=1}^{t} v_i\,(k_i^{\top}q_t)=\Big(\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{t} v_i k_i^{\top}}_{S_t}\Big)q_t,\qquad S_t=S_{t-1}+v_t k_t^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v\times d_k}
blocks.caption: The state S_t is a running sum of outer products. Each step adds one rank-1 matrix and reads the output as S_t times q_t: an RNN with a matrix-valued hidden state.

blocks.md:
A toy with $d_k=d_v=2$ and four tokens (numbers chosen by hand):

- keys $k$: (1,0), (0,1), (1,1), (1,0)
- values $v$: (1,2), (3,0), (0,1), (2,2)
- queries $q$: (1,0), (1,1), (0,1), (1,1)

Rows of $S$ index value dimensions, columns index key dimensions.

blocks.title: The 2 x 2 state S_t after each token

scenes.caption: Start: S_0 is all zeros. Nothing has been written.
Token 1 adds v k^T = (1,2)(1,0)^T, filling column 1. Output o_1 = S_1 q_1 = (1,2).
Token 2 adds (3,0)(0,1)^T into column 2. With q_2 = (1,1), o_2 sums both columns: (4,2).
Token 3 has key (1,1), so (0,1) is added to both columns. o_3 = S_3 (0,1) = (3,1).
Token 4 adds (2,2) to column 1 again. o_4 = S_4 (1,1) = (6,6). The state never grew: still 4 numbers after 4 tokens.

blocks.prompt: Training wants all outputs at once, not a loop. Compute token 4's output the attention way: weights $k_i^\top q_4$ for i = 1..4, then the weighted sum of values. Do you get (6,6)?
blocks.reveal: Weights are $k_i^\top(1,1)$ = 1, 1, 2, 1. Weighted sum: 1(1,2) + 1(3,0) + 2(0,1) + 1(2,2) = **(6,6)**, the same as $S_4q_4$. The parallel form $O=(QK^\top\odot M)V$ and the recurrent form compute identical numbers; only the order of operations differs.

blocks.title: Parallel form: masked QK^T, compared with softmax

scenes.caption: Linear attention weights: QK^T with the causal mask M zeroing the future. Multiplying by V gives rows (1,2), (4,2), (3,1), (6,6), matching the recurrence.
Row 4 sums to 5, not 1: without softmax or the denominator, weights are raw dot products. Nothing forces them to be a probability distribution.
For contrast, softmax of the same scores divided by sqrt(2): row 4 becomes 0.20, 0.20, 0.40, 0.20. Softmax sharpens and normalizes; no finite d x d state can reproduce it exactly.

blocks.md: Linear attention is one function with two schedules: a **parallel form** $O=(QK^\top\odot M)V$ that is matmul-friendly for training, and a **recurrent form** $S_t=S_{t-1}+v_tk_t^\top$, $o_t=S_tq_t$ with constant time and memory per generated token.

Linear attention is not a cheap approximation of softmax attention that converges to it. The exponential kernel has an infinite-dimensional feature map (Katharopoulos et al.), so any finite state is a different, weaker model. That gap is what the rest of this course is about.

blocks.question: A linear-attention layer with $d_k=d_v=128$ per head has generated 10,000 tokens. What does it need to keep per head to generate token 10,001?
options: All 10,000 keys and values, like a KV cache
The 128 x 128 state matrix S
Only the last 128 keys
The full 10,000 x 10,000 attention matrix
blocks.explain: Everything the layer knows about the past is folded into $S_t$, a 128 x 128 matrix (16,384 numbers) regardless of how many tokens came before. That is the RNN view of linear attention.

blocks.question: Why does regrouping $(QK^\top)V$ as $Q(K^\top V)$ fail for softmax attention?
options: Matrix multiplication is not associative
The softmax is applied to each row of $QK^\top$ before multiplying by V, so the product cannot be regrouped
Softmax attention uses different key and query dimensions
The causal mask makes regrouping impossible for any attention
blocks.explain: Associativity only holds for plain products. Softmax applies a nonlinear exp and normalization to every entry of $QK^\top$ first. Causal masking alone is fine: the running sum $S_t$ handles it.

lessons.title: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up

blocks.md: Schlag, Irie and Schmidhuber (2021) showed linear attention is a **fast weight programmer**: $S$ is a weight matrix that the network rewrites at every token by adding outer products $v_tk_t^\top$, and reading $Sq$ is a lookup. Think of $S$ as an associative memory: store value $v$ under key $k$, retrieve by presenting a key.

blocks.caption: Reading with key k_j returns v_j exactly if k_j has unit length and is orthogonal to every other stored key. Any overlap k_i^T k_j leaks v_i into the answer.

blocks.md:
Toy memory with $d_k=2$ and scalar values ($d_v=1$, so $S$ is a 1 x 2 row). Keys have unit length:

- $k_A=(1,0)$, $k_B=(0,1)$, $k_C=(0.6,0.8)$

The sequence writes A=4, then B=2, then **rewrites** A=1 (the fact changed), then writes C=3. A perfect memory would finally return 1, 2, 3.

blocks.prompt: After the rewrite A=1, the state is $S=4k_A^\top+2k_B^\top+1k_A^\top$. What does reading with $k_A$ return?
blocks.reveal: **5**, not 1. Linear attention can only add: the old value 4 and the new value 1 are summed. There is no instruction for "replace what is stored under this key".

blocks.title: Linear attention memory: reads after each write

scenes.caption: Write A=4: S = (4,0). k_A reads 4. k_C = (0.6,0.8) already reads 2.4 because it overlaps k_A by 0.6.
Write B=2: S = (4,2). k_A and k_B are orthogonal, so both read back exactly: 4 and 2.
Rewrite A=1: S = (5,2). k_A now reads 5, the sum of old and new. Additive memory cannot overwrite.
Write C=3: S = (6.8,4.4). Every read is now wrong (6.8, 4.4, 7.6 instead of 1, 2, 3): the third key cannot be orthogonal to the first two in 2 dimensions.

blocks.md:
Two separate failures showed up:

1. **No overwrite.** Rewriting a key accumulates values instead of replacing them.
2. **Collisions.** At most $d_k$ keys can be mutually orthogonal. Once a head has seen more distinct keys than its key dimension, stored values become superimposed. Schlag et al. call this the memory capacity limitation, and the Gated DeltaNet paper notes that collisions become inevitable once the sequence is longer than the dimension.

This is why early linear Transformers trailed softmax attention on language modeling and especially on **in-context recall** (find a fact stated earlier in the prompt). Softmax attention keeps every key separately and can pick one out sharply; a fixed $d_k \times d_v$ state must compress.

The state is a key-value memory with room for about $d_k$ clean associations per head. Linear attention writes to it with a purely additive rule, so it can neither correct an old association nor make room for new ones.
Bigger is not a free fix. Raising $d_k$ raises capacity, but state size and per-token compute grow as $d_k d_v$. The research direction instead is a smarter write rule, which is the next lesson.

blocks.question: A head has $d_k=64$. A prompt states 500 different key facts, each with its own key direction. What happens to recall under plain linear attention?
options: Nothing, because 500 tokens is short
Keys cannot all be orthogonal in 64 dimensions, so reads mix many stored values
Only the last 64 facts are kept and older ones are cleanly deleted
The model switches to softmax attention automatically
blocks.explain: At most 64 directions can be mutually orthogonal. With 500 associations the overlaps $k_i^\top k_j$ are nonzero and every read returns a weighted mixture. Nothing is cleanly deleted either: additive memory never forgets.

blocks.question: In the toy, why did $k_A$ and $k_B$ read back perfectly after the first two writes?
options: Because they were written first
Because the values 4 and 2 are small
Because the keys are unit length and orthogonal, so $k_A^\top k_B = 0$ and nothing leaks
Because S was reset between writes
blocks.explain: Reading $Sk_A = 4(k_A^\top k_A) + 2(k_B^\top k_A) = 4\cdot 1 + 2\cdot 0 = 4$. Orthonormal keys make the memory exact; overlap is what causes interference.

lessons.title: The delta rule: overwrite instead of add

blocks.md: DeltaNet (Schlag et al. 2021, scaled up by Yang et al. 2024) replaces the additive write with the **delta rule**, also called the Widrow-Hoff rule from 1960. Before writing, it reads what memory currently returns for the key, $v^{\text{old}}_t=S_{t-1}k_t$. It then blends in the new value with a **writing strength** $\beta_t\in(0,1)$, computed per token as $\beta_t=\sigma(W_\beta x_t)$, and swaps it in:

blocks.caption: Remove the old value stored under k_t, write the new one. With beta = 1 the old value is fully replaced; with beta = 0 the memory is unchanged.

blocks.md:
The same update is one step of **online gradient descent** on a regression loss: make the memory map $k_t$ to $v_t$.

$\mathcal{L}_t(S)=\tfrac12\lVert Sk_t-v_t\rVert^2$, and $S_t=S_{t-1}-\beta_t\nabla\mathcal{L}_t=S_{t-1}-\beta_t(S_{t-1}k_t-v_t)k_t^\top$.

The "delta" is the prediction error $v_t-S_{t-1}k_t$. Plain linear attention, by contrast, optimizes the linear loss $-\langle Sk_t,v_t\rangle$, which rewards adding $v_t$ no matter what is already stored.

blocks.title: Same writes, delta rule with beta = 1

scenes.caption: Write A=4: memory was empty so v_old = 0 and S = (4,0), the same as linear attention.
Write B=2: v_old = S k_B = 0, S = (4,2). Still identical to linear attention, because k_B is orthogonal to everything stored.
Rewrite A=1: v_old = S k_A = 4, the error is 1 - 4 = -3, so S = (4,2) - 3(1,0) = (1,2). k_A now reads 1, and k_B is untouched at 2.
Write C=3: v_old = 2.2, error 0.8, S = (1.48,2.64). k_C reads exactly 3. The fix along k_C nudges k_A to 1.48 and k_B to 2.64: three keys still collide in 2 dimensions.

blocks.md: The delta rule makes writes **targeted**: it changes $S$ only along the direction $k_t$ (the matrix $I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top$ leaves every direction orthogonal to $k_t$ alone) and by exactly the amount needed to correct the error. It fixes the no-overwrite failure; it cannot raise capacity above $d_k$.

blocks.prompt: Rerun the same four writes with $\beta=0.5$ instead of 1. After the first write (A=4), what does $k_A$ read?
blocks.reveal: **2**. With $\beta=0.5$ the new value is halfway between the old (0) and the target (4). After all four writes the reads are 1.89, 1.52 and 2.35: each write only moves halfway. The model learns $\beta_t$ per token, so it can choose a strong overwrite for important tokens and a light touch for others.

blocks.md: **Stability.** The transition matrix $I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top$ is a generalized Householder matrix. Its eigenvalues are 1 (with multiplicity $d-1$) and $1-\beta_t\lVert k_t\rVert^2$. If that last eigenvalue leaves $[-1,1]$, repeated writes blow up the state. Schlag et al. normalized keys with the L1 norm for this reason; Yang et al. use L2 normalization instead, so $\lVert k_t\rVert=1$ and the eigenvalue $1-\beta_t$ stays in $[0,1]$. With $\beta_t=1$ the matrix becomes a projection that erases one direction and keeps the other $d-1$.

Forgetting to normalize keys is a real bug, not a detail. Take $k_C$ scaled to length 2 and $\beta=1$: the eigenvalue is $1-4=-3$, so a component along that key is multiplied by -3, 9, -27, 81, -243 over five repeated writes.

Why was DeltaNet not used at scale before 2024? Its original training algorithm was strictly sequential over the sequence, which uses GPUs poorly. Yang et al. (NeurIPS 2024) found a chunkwise parallel algorithm (lesson 5), trained a 1.3B-parameter DeltaNet on 100B tokens, and reported better perplexity and zero-shot results than Mamba and GLA baselines.

blocks.question: Memory holds $k_A\to4$ and $k_B\to2$ with orthogonal unit keys. A token writes $k_A\to1$ with $\beta=1$ using the delta rule. What does $k_B$ read afterwards?
blocks.explain: The update only changes $S$ along $k_A$: $S(I-k_Ak_A^\top)$ leaves the $k_B$ direction untouched because $k_A^\top k_B=0$. So $k_B$ still reads 2, while $k_A$ now reads exactly 1.

blocks.question: Which statement about DeltaNet's $\beta_t$ is correct?
options: It is a fixed hyperparameter shared by all tokens
It is a per-token learning rate in (0,1) for an online regression step
It decays all of memory uniformly at each step
It must equal the norm of the key
blocks.explain: $\beta_t=\sigma(W_\beta x_t)$ is computed from the token, and in the gradient-descent view it is the step size. Uniform decay of all memory is a different mechanism (the gate $\alpha_t$ in the next lesson).

lessons.title: Gated DeltaNet: targeted writes plus fast forgetting

blocks.md: A second family of fixes added a **decay gate**. Mamba2 (a selective state-space model), written as linear attention, uses $S_t=\alpha_tS_{t-1}+v_tk_t^\top$ where $\alpha_t\in(0,1)$ is computed from the token. Every association shrinks by the same factor each step. That clears memory quickly, but it is untargeted: to forget one stale fact, everything fades equally.

blocks.title: How long a memory survives under a constant gate

scenes.caption: alpha = 0.99: half of an association is gone after about 69 tokens, and 0.37 of it remains after 100.
alpha = 0.9: half-life about 6.6 tokens; after 20 tokens only 0.12 remains. Fine for clearing a finished document, fatal for a fact needed later.
alpha = 0.999: half-life about 693 tokens. Real models compute alpha per token, so they can hold near 1 and drop toward 0 at a boundary (simplified: constant here).

blocks.md: The Gated DeltaNet paper (Yang, Kautz, Hatamizadeh, ICLR 2025) observes the two fixes are complementary: **gating enables rapid erasure, the delta rule enables targeted updates.** The gated delta rule simply multiplies the delta transition by $\alpha_t$:

blocks.caption: Equation 10 of the paper. alpha_t near 0 wipes the memory; alpha_t = 1 recovers pure DeltaNet; beta_t still controls how strongly the new key-value pair overwrites.

blocks.md: A context-switch toy. Document 1 writes $k_A\to4$ and $k_B\to2$. Document 2 begins and writes $k_A\to1$; on that token we set $\alpha=0.1$ by hand (a trained model would learn to). Document 2 never mentions B, so ideally $k_A$ reads 1 and $k_B$ reads 0. All rules use $\beta=1$ and the unit keys from before.

blocks.title: After the context switch: four update rules

scenes.caption: End of document 1: every rule holds S = (4,2), so k_A reads 4 and k_B reads 2.
Linear adds: k_A = 5, k_B = 2 stale. Mamba2-style decays then adds: k_A = 0.4 + 1 = 1.4. DeltaNet overwrites A exactly but keeps stale B = 2.
Gated DeltaNet decays to (0.4,0.2), then the delta step corrects A from 0.4 to exactly 1. Result: k_A = 1, k_B = 0.2. Only it gets both right (alpha = 0 would give 0).

blocks.title: The gated delta rule as a loop
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def gated_delta(keys, vals, alphas, betas):
    S = np.zeros(2)        # d_v = 1, d_k = 2
    for k, v, a, b in zip(keys, vals, alphas, betas):
        S = a * S          # gate: decay all memory
        v_old = S @ k      # what memory says for k
        S = S + b * (v - v_old) * k  # delta step
    return S

kA, kB = np.array([1., 0.]), np.array([0., 1.])
S = gated_delta([kA, kB, kA], [4., 2., 1.],
                alphas=[1., 1., 0.1], betas=[1., 1., 1.])
print(S @ kA, S @ kB)

scenes.caption: Token 1 (k_A, v = 4, alpha = 1): nothing to decay, v_old = 0, so the delta step writes 4 along k_A.
Token 2 (k_B, v = 2, alpha = 1): v_old = S @ k_B = 0, so 2 is written along k_B.
Token 3 (k_A, v = 1, alpha = 0.1): the gate shrinks S to [0.4, 0.2].
v_old = 0.4. The delta step adds (1 - 0.4) along k_A, giving [1.0, 0.2].
Reads: k_A gives 1.0, k_B gives 0.2. Real kernels do the same per head with S of shape d_v x d_k and vector values.

blocks.md: **Online-learning view.** Table 1 of the paper writes each rule as minimizing a per-token objective. DeltaNet minimizes $\lVert S_t-S_{t-1}\rVert_F^2-2\langle S_tk_t,\beta_t(v_t-S_{t-1}k_t)\rangle$; Gated DeltaNet replaces $S_{t-1}$ with $\alpha_tS_{t-1}$. In the SGD picture, $\beta_t$ is the learning rate and $\alpha_t$ is an adaptive **weight decay** on the fast weights.

blocks.title: Single needle in a haystack, 1.3B models (paper Table 2)

scenes.caption: S-NIAH-1 at 8K tokens (pass-key in repeated filler): DeltaNet 98.8, Mamba2 30.4, Gated DeltaNet 91.8. Uniform decay forgets the needle.
S-NIAH-2 at 4K tokens (number hidden in real essays): 18.6, 56.2, 92.2. Without gating DeltaNet's memory fills with essay text and collides.
S-NIAH-3 at 2K tokens (UUID value in essays): 47.0, 47.6, 84.2. Memorizing a complex value needs both clearing and precise writes.

nodes.label:
q, k: linear,
short conv, SiLU

gated delta rule
S update, o = S q

scenes.caption: Queries, keys and values come from linear projections, a short causal convolution and SiLU. q and k are L2-normalized for stability (lesson 3).
alpha and beta come from plain linear projections. In the reference code beta = sigmoid(.) and alpha = exp(g) with g = -exp(A_log) softplus(. + dt_bias), Mamba2's parameterization.
The output is normalized, multiplied by a SiLU output gate and projected. Blocks alternate with SwiGLU MLPs in a Llama-style stack.

blocks.md: Gated DeltaNet's one-line change: decay first with a data-dependent $\alpha_t$, then do a delta-rule write with $\beta_t$. $\alpha_t\to0$ clears memory at a context switch; $\alpha_t\to1$ keeps it and lets the delta rule edit single associations.

blocks.question: A model reads a long code file, then a new unrelated file starts. Which mechanism lets a Gated DeltaNet head discard the old file's associations within a few tokens?
options: The delta rule with $\beta_t=1$
L2 normalization of keys
A small $\alpha_t$ at the boundary
The short convolution
blocks.explain: The delta rule only edits the direction of the current key, one association per token, so it cannot clear thousands of stale associations quickly. A small $\alpha_t$ scales the whole state toward zero at once.

blocks.question: In S-NIAH-1 (needle in repeated filler) at 8K, Mamba2 scores 30.4 and DeltaNet 98.8. What is the best explanation?
options: Mamba2's state is smaller
Mamba2 decays all associations every step, so the needle fades over thousands of filler tokens; DeltaNet never decays
DeltaNet uses softmax attention for long inputs
The filler text collides with the needle in DeltaNet only
blocks.explain: The paper's own reading: decay hurts retention. Repeated filler adds little new information, so DeltaNet's lack of forgetting is harmless here, while uniform decay erodes the needle. Gated DeltaNet (91.8) loses a little because it also decays.

lessons.title: Chunkwise training and hybrid models in production

blocks.md:
Training processes whole sequences, so we want parallel matmuls. Yang et al. (2024) compare three ways to compute the same layer for sequence length $L$, head dimension $d$, chunk size $C$:

- **Parallel form** $(QK^\top\odot M)V$: $O(L^2d+Ld^2)$ FLOPs, all positions at once.
- **Recurrent form**: $O(Ld^2)$ FLOPs but $L$ sequential steps of small elementwise work that cannot use tensor cores.
- **Chunkwise form**: $O(LCd+Ld^2)$ FLOPs and $L/C$ sequential steps. $C=L$ recovers the parallel form, $C=1$ the recurrent one; in practice $C$ is 64 or 128.

blocks.title: FLOP counts of the three forms (constants dropped)

curves.label: chunkwise: L C d + L d^2

scenes.caption: At L = 4096, d = 128, C = 64: parallel about 2.2e9, chunkwise about 1.0e8, recurrent about 6.7e7. Parallel grows quadratically.
Chunkwise stays within a small constant of the recurrent FLOPs, yet needs only L/C = 64 sequential steps at L = 4096 instead of 4096.
show: chunkwise: L C d + L d^2

scenes.caption: Larger chunks add intra-chunk work (the L C d term) in exchange for fewer sequential steps; C = L would be the parallel form again.

blocks.md: For plain linear attention the chunkwise form is easy: inside a chunk use the masked parallel form, across chunks pass the state $S_{[t+1]}=S_{[t]}+V_{[t]}^\top K_{[t]}$. The delta rule is harder because each chunk's transition is a product of $C$ Householder-like matrices $\prod(I-\beta_ik_ik_i^\top)$, and materializing a $d\times d$ state per token would cost too much memory traffic.

Yang et al. use the classical **WY representation**: a product of such matrices equals $I-\sum_i w_ik_i^\top$ for vectors $w_i$ computable from the chunk's keys. A **UT transform** gets all $w_i$ (and matching $u_i$ for values) by inverting one small $C\times C$ lower-triangular matrix, so the work becomes matmuls. Gated DeltaNet extends this by folding the cumulative decay products $\gamma$ of $\alpha_t$ into the same matrices, adding little overhead.

blocks.title: Chunkwise schedule for one head, L = 256, C = 64 (simplified)

scenes.caption: Recurrent form: 256 tiny dependent updates, one after another. Few FLOPs, poor GPU use. Time axis is schematic, not measured.
Chunkwise step 1: all four chunks build their WY/UT factors (w, u) in parallel with dense matmuls.
Step 2: the only sequential part. The state is carried across 4 chunk boundaries (L/C = 4 steps) instead of 256 tokens.
Step 3: every chunk computes its outputs in parallel from its incoming state plus intra-chunk attention. FLA's kernel follows this split: intra-chunk WY, state pass, then outputs.

blocks.md: Training uses the chunkwise kernel; decoding uses the recurrent form, one $S$ update per token. FLA's `GatedDeltaNet` layer switches automatically: chunk mode for training and long prefills, a fused recurrent kernel for short inference inputs (64 tokens or fewer).

**Hybrids.** A fixed state still cannot match attention at exact recall, so the paper also builds hybrids: **H1** interleaves Gated DeltaNet with sliding-window attention (window 2K), **H2** stacks Mamba2, Gated DeltaNet and sliding-window attention. Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B ships this idea: its config has 48 layers laid out as 12 repeats of (3 Gated DeltaNet + 1 gated full-attention), each followed by an MoE layer. Kimi Linear similarly mixes KDA, a Gated DeltaNet variant with finer-grained gating, with full MLA (multi-head latent attention, which caches a compressed latent instead of full keys and values) layers.

blocks.title: Per-sequence cache in Qwen3-Next vs an all-attention variant

scenes.caption: From the config: attention layers have 2 KV heads of dim 256, so 2 x 2 x 256 x 2 bytes = 2 KiB per token per layer. An all-attention 48-layer variant (hypothetical) needs 96 KiB per token.

Hybrid = 12 attention layers (24 KiB per token) plus a fixed Gated DeltaNet state: 36 layers x 32 heads x 128 x 128 numbers = 72 MiB at 4 bytes. At 256K tokens: 6,216 vs 24,576 MiB. Simplified: ignores conv state.
Average zero-shot commonsense accuracy: 52.25, 54.89, 52.14, 55.32, 56.40, 56.18. Gated DeltaNet beats the other recurrent models; hybrids are best.
Average real-world recall (inputs truncated to 2K): 37.0, 29.8, 26.2, 30.6, 39.0, 40.1. Pure recurrent models still trail attention; adding attention layers closes the gap.

blocks.md: Do not read "linear" as "free". The paper measures Gated DeltaNet training throughput as essentially equal to DeltaNet but slightly below Mamba2, because its transition matrices are more expressive. And a pure linear model still loses to attention on recall-heavy tasks; production systems keep some attention layers.

blocks.question: You must train a Gated DeltaNet layer on 8K-token sequences on GPUs. Which computation form should the training kernel use?
options: Recurrent form, because it has the fewest FLOPs
Fully parallel form, because it has no sequential steps
Chunkwise form, which keeps FLOPs near linear and turns most work into matmuls with only L/C sequential steps
Any form, they run equally fast
blocks.explain: The recurrent form serializes 8K small updates and cannot use tensor cores well; the parallel form pays $O(L^2d)$ FLOPs. Chunkwise is what FLA and the paper use for training.

blocks.question: Qwen3-Next's context grows from 32K to 256K tokens. Which part of its per-sequence cache grows?
options: Only the KV cache of the 12 full-attention layers; the Gated DeltaNet state stays 72 MiB
Only the Gated DeltaNet state
Both grow 8x
Neither grows
blocks.explain: Gated DeltaNet layers keep a fixed $d_k\times d_v$ state per head regardless of length. The attention layers' KV cache grows linearly: 768 MiB at 32K to 6,144 MiB at 256K, while the 72 MiB state is unchanged.
